course_title: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
chapter_title: High-Level Design: Identifying Core Components and APIs
chapter_summary:
With a clear understanding of the problem's requirements and a quantitative grasp of its scale, you're ready to move into the high-level design phase. This is where you start sketching the blueprint of your system, identifying the major architectural blocks and how they interact. The goal here is not to delve into intricate details but to establish a robust, scalable, and coherent overall structure. Think of it as drawing a city map before designing individual buildings; you identify major roads, districts, and key landmarks first. This phase typically involves drawing a block diagram on a whiteboard or shared drawing tool, explaining each component's role, and justifying your choices based on the earlier requirements and estimations.

Every distributed system typically starts with a client (web browser, mobile app, IoT device) making requests. These requests usually first hit a **Load Balancer**. A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers, ensuring no single server becomes a bottleneck and improving overall system availability and responsiveness. It can also perform health checks, routing, and SSL termination. Behind the load balancer, you'll find your **Web Servers** (or API Servers). These are the entry points for your application logic, handling user requests, processing business logic, and interacting with other services. They are typically stateless to allow for easy horizontal scaling.

For data storage, you'll need one or more **Databases**. The choice between SQL (relational) and NoSQL (non-relational) databases depends heavily on your data model, consistency requirements, and scalability needs.
*   **SQL Databases** (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL): Excellent for structured data, complex queries, and strong ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). Often used for critical transactional data.
*   **NoSQL Databases:** Offer flexibility, high scalability, and availability. Types include:
    *   **Key-Value Stores** (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB): Simple, fast lookups.
    *   **Document Databases** (e.g., MongoDB, Couchbase): Flexible schema, good for semi-structured data.
    *   **Column-Family Stores** (e.g., Cassandra, HBase): Highly scalable for large datasets, good for time-series data.
    *   **Graph Databases** (e.g., Neo4j): Ideal for highly interconnected data (e.g., social networks).
You must justify your database choice based on the data types, read/write patterns, and consistency requirements.

To improve performance and reduce database load, **Caches** are essential. A cache stores frequently accessed data in faster, temporary storage (often RAM). Common caching layers include client-side caches, CDN caches, and server-side caches (e.g., Redis, Memcached). For asynchronous processing, decoupling services, and handling bursts of traffic, **Message Queues** (e.g., Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) are invaluable. They allow services to communicate asynchronously, improving fault tolerance and scalability. For example, when a user uploads a video, the web server might simply put a message on a queue, and a separate video processing service consumes that message to handle encoding.

Let's apply this to our URL Shortener example:
*   **Client:** User's browser or mobile app.
*   **Load Balancer:** Distributes requests to web servers.
*   **Web Servers (API Service):**
    *   `POST /shorten`: Takes a long URL, generates a unique short code, stores it, and returns the short URL.
    *   `GET /{short_code}`: Looks up the short code, retrieves the long URL, and redirects.
*   **Cache (e.g., Redis):** Stores frequently accessed `short_code -> long_url` mappings to reduce database load and improve redirection latency.
*   **Database (e.g., MySQL or Cassandra):** Stores the mapping of `short_code -> long_url`. If using MySQL, consider sharding for scalability. If using Cassandra, it's inherently distributed.
*   **(Optional) Analytics Service:** An asynchronous service that consumes messages from a queue (e.g., Kafka) about redirection events to count clicks.

When defining APIs, focus on RESTful principles for simplicity and widespread adoption. For example, for the URL Shortener:
*   `POST /api/v1/urls` with JSON body `{"longUrl": "https://verylongurl.com/..."}`
    *   Returns `201 Created` with JSON body `{"shortUrl": "http://short.ly/abcde"}`
*   `GET /abcde`
    *   Returns `302 Found` with `Location: https://verylongurl.com/...` header.

Common mistakes in this phase include drawing an overly complex diagram with too many microservices without justification, or conversely, designing a monolithic system that clearly won't scale. Another pitfall is not considering data partitioning or replication for databases, assuming a single database instance will suffice. Always start simple, add complexity as needed, and justify each component based on the requirements and estimations.

screens.title: High-Level Design: Identify Core Components and APIs
screens.subtitle: Sketch the system blueprint using components justified by requirements and scale

narration.text: In this lesson we move from clarified requirements and traffic estimates to a high-level blueprint that guides all later design decisions. You will learn how to name and place core components — load balancers, web servers, caches, databases, and message queues — and how to justify each one based on traffic patterns, latency needs, and failure modes. High-level design is not about implementation details; it is about choosing the right building blocks and showing how they interact. For example, a load balancer protects the web tier from spikes, caches reduce read load on persistent stores, and queues decouple synchronous user-facing work from heavy background processing. We will use a URL shortener example and a notification service exercise to practice mapping endpoints to components and selecting storage technologies. As you study these blueprints, pay attention to common mistakes: adding microservices without need, or assuming a single database will scale. By the end you will be able to explain why each component exists, propose A P I endpoints that match responsibilities, and defend your choices with simple performance and scaling rationale. How would you justify one component choice for a system you know well?

keyIdea.title: Design as a blueprint, not code
keyIdea.text: High-level design defines major components and their interactions so you can reason about scale, fault tolerance, and API responsibilities before implementation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus your work in high-level design. First, you will translate clarified requirements and scale estimates into a clear block diagram that shows the major components and their interactions; this skill matters because it turns vague needs into a defendable architecture. Second, you will identify core components like load balancers, web servers, databases, caches, and message queues and explain why each is necessary for availability or latency. Third, you will learn the purpose and typical placement of each component so you can place them in a coherent layout — for example, putting caches close to the web tier to reduce database load. Finally, you will define key A P I endpoints and communication patterns that reflect responsibilities and allow independent scaling. Each objective ties to an interview task: show your diagram, name the bottlenecks, and propose one concrete improvement. Practice by explaining your choices aloud, and you will find your designs become easier to defend and iterate.

keyIdea.text: Translate needs and scale into components and APIs you can defend, focusing on availability, latency, and justifiable complexity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Practice & Defense)
screens.subtitle: Translate designs into defendable choices and interview talking points

narration.text: This screen reinforces how to practice and defend the design choices you made. For each objective you will practice a short verbal justification: explain why you chose a load balancer, why a certain database type fits the access pattern, and why you introduced a queue or cache. Practicing this defense matters because interviewers often probe motivation, trade-offs, and alternatives. A strong defense shows you can reason about availability, durability, and performance, not just draw boxes. Use simple mnemonics like Map → Place → Define to keep your explanation structured, and prepare one example where you remove a component to show the cost of that simplification. For hands-on practice, follow the notification service exercise: draw a diagram, label APIs, and write a one-paragraph justification for the queue. This prepares you to explain trade-offs succinctly and respond when an interviewer asks about a different scale or failure mode.

screens.title: From Requirements to a High-Level Diagram
screens.subtitle: Turn needs and scale into a simple block diagram you can explain

narration.text: High-level design starts once requirements and scale are clear. The primary goal is to produce a block diagram that communicates intent: which components are necessary, where bottlenecks might appear, and how data flows between parts. A practical approach is to begin with clients, draw a load balancer, then the web/A P I tier, and finally persistent and asynchronous components. For example, if you expect many more reads than writes, sketch a cache between the web servers and the database to absorb read traffic. If you see bursts of heavy background processing, place a message queue so workers can process asynchronously. When you justify a component, tie it to a measurable requirement — latency target, expected requests per second, or durability need — rather than a vague belief that "it seems safer." A common misconception is to add many microservices early; keep things coarse-grained until you can justify splitting. As a closing prompt, when you draw a diagram for an app you know, ask: which component would fail first under a spike, and how would you mitigate it? That question focuses your next design choice.

keyIdea.title: Diagram with intent
keyIdea.text: A block diagram should map directly to requirements and expose where scaling and failure handling are needed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › From Requirements to a High-Level Diagram
Definition & approach

High-level design is a readable blueprint that maps requirements and scale estimates to components and data flow. Start coarse and only split components when justified by requirements.

Step 1
Identify clients and expected traffic
Estimate requests per second and peak patterns to inform capacity and caching.
Step 2
Choose core components
Select load balancer, web tier, storage, caches, and queues when needed to meet targets.
Step 3
Annotate responsibilities
Label APIs and which component owns each piece of logic to avoid confusion later.
Key Takeaway

Keep diagrams tied to measurable requirements; avoid premature microservice decomposition.

Annotated example
Client → Load Balancer

Web/API Servers (stateless)
Handle business logic; keep them stateless so you can scale horizontally.
Cache layer
Reduce read load for hot data to meet latency targets.
Persistent store & queues
Databases for durable storage and queues for asynchronous processing.

screens.title: Load Balancer: Role and Responsibilities
screens.subtitle: Why traffic distribution and health checks are essential

narration.text: A load balancer is the system's traffic gatekeeper. It distributes incoming requests across multiple servers to avoid overloading a single instance and to improve overall availability. Beyond simple round-robin distribution, load balancers often perform health checks to detect failed servers and route traffic away from them. They may also handle SSL termination to offload cryptographic work from the web servers. In an interview, you should be able to state why a load balancer is present: it smooths spikes, enables rolling upgrades by draining nodes, and acts as the first point to apply routing rules. A common misconception is that a load balancer alone guarantees availability; it helps, but your backend services and persistence layers must also be designed to scale. For a concrete example, in a URL shortener, the load balancer takes browser redirect requests and distributes them across stateless A P I servers that perform the lookup, keeping latency low even under high read rates. Ask yourself: what health checks and routing policies would you choose for a real service? Load Balancer: Role and Responsibilities means load balancers prevent single-node bottlenecks, enable graceful maintenance, and centralize routing decisions for the web tier.. In practical terms, why traffic distribution and health checks are essential. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Traffic distribution matters
keyIdea.text: Load balancers prevent single-node bottlenecks, enable graceful maintenance, and centralize routing decisions for the web tier.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Load Balancer
Core responsibilities
  • Distribute incoming network traffic across multiple servers to avoid overload.
  • Perform health checks and route around unhealthy instances.
  • Optionally offload SSL termination and implement routing rules.
Example
In a URL shortener, the load balancer handles redirect traffic and spreads the lookup load across the API servers to keep latency low.
Key Takeaway

Choose a load balancer and health checks that reflect failure modes and maintenance patterns in your system.

Common mistakes & pro tip
Mistake
Assuming the load balancer alone solves availability when backups and data replication are also necessary.
Pro tip
Use health checks that validate application-level readiness, not only TCP port openness.

screens.title: Web Servers and Stateless API Services
screens.subtitle: Why statelessness enables horizontal scaling

narration.text: Web servers or A P I servers are the application’s entry point for business logic. They receive client requests, execute logic such as validation or short-lived computation, and interact with persistence or downstream services. Designing these servers to be stateless — that is, not storing session-specific data locally — is a foundational practice because it allows instances to be added or removed without complex synchronization. When state is required, delegate it to external stores like databases or caches. For instance, a URL shortener's A P I servers generate short codes and write them to the database, while using a cache for frequent lookups. A typical misconception is that statelessness requires no storage; rather, it requires that any state necessary for user sessions or transactions lives in managed services so any instance can handle any request. When designing APIs, ensure that endpoints are small and map clearly to responsibilities to keep servers simple and horizontally scalable. Ask yourself: where would I store session data in a system that must handle many concurrent users? Web Servers and Stateless API Services means stateless web servers let you scale horizontally; offload session and long-term state to dedicated stores.. In practical terms, why statelessness enables horizontal scaling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stateless => scalable
keyIdea.text: Stateless web servers let you scale horizontally; offload session and long-term state to dedicated stores.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Web Servers & Stateless Services
Role

Web servers execute business logic for incoming requests. Keep them stateless so instances can be replaced or scaled without migrating user session data.

Pattern
When state exists, place it in caches or databases that are independent of any single server.
Example
API servers for a URL shortener store mappings in a DB and use Redis for fast redirect lookups.
Key Takeaway

Stateless services simplify scaling and allow easy horizontal growth under load.

Anti-patterns & guidance
Anti-pattern
Storing session state in local server memory, which prevents elastic scaling and complicates failover.
Guidance
Use external session stores or stateless tokens and keep APIs focused and idempotent where possible.

screens.title: Databases: SQL vs NoSQL — choosing by access pattern
screens.subtitle: Match data model and consistency to storage technology

narration.text: Choosing between S Q L and NoSQL depends on the shape of your data and the guarantees you need. S Q L databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL excel at structured data, complex queries, and strong ACID properties, making them suitable for transactional workloads such as orders and payments. NoSQL systems trade some of that strict consistency for scalability and flexible schemas. Key-value stores give you fast lookups for session caches, document databases suit semi-structured records, column-family stores scale for time-series or massive write loads, and graph databases handle highly connected data. The right choice is determined by read/write patterns and consistency needs. For instance, a URL shortener can use MySQL for strict mappings and sharding as traffic grows, or use a distributed NoSQL like Cassandra if you need high write throughput and eventual consistency. A common misconception is that NoSQL always scales better; design and operational complexity vary by system. When you pick a database, state the access pattern and why the chosen database aligns with it. Databases: SQL vs NoSQL — choosing by access pattern means select storage based on data structure, read/write patterns, and required consistency — justify with concrete access characteristics.. In practical terms, match data model and consistency to storage technology. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match store to access
keyIdea.text: Select storage based on data structure, read/write patterns, and required consistency — justify with concrete access characteristics.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Databases: SQL vs NoSQL
SQL Databases

Use SQL for structured, transactional data that benefits from strong consistency and complex queries.

When to choose
Critical transactions, relational queries, and where ACID guarantees are required.
NoSQL Options

Choose a NoSQL type by access pattern: key-value for fast lookups, document for flexible records, column-family for time-series scale, graph for connected data.

When to choose
High scale with relaxed consistency, flexible schemas, or specialized access patterns like graphs.

screens.title: NoSQL Families and When to Use Each
screens.subtitle: Key-value, document, column-family and graph stores explained

narration.text: NoSQL is a family of storage systems optimized for different patterns. Key-value stores like Redis or DynamoDB offer simple, extremely fast lookups and are ideal for session caches or mapping keys to small payloads. Document databases store semi-structured records and are useful when records vary in shape, such as user profiles. Column-family stores like Cassandra are designed for horizontal scale and high write throughput, making them a fit for time-series or event logs. Graph databases like Neo4j are specialized for traversing relationships, useful for social graphs and recommendation tasks. When you choose among these, describe the read/write ratio, the query patterns, and your consistency tolerance. A subtle misconception is to assume one NoSQL type fits all needs within a project; in large systems you often use multiple stores for different data shapes. The practical takeaway is to pair each dataset with the storage model that reduces complexity and meets your latency and durability goals. NoSQL Families and When to Use Each means pick the nosql flavor that maps to your query patterns: key-value for lookups, document for flexible records, column-family for scale, graph for relationships.. In practical terms, key-value, document, column-family and graph stores explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NoSQL is multiple tools
keyIdea.text: Pick the NoSQL flavor that maps to your query patterns: key-value for lookups, document for flexible records, column-family for scale, graph for relationships.

Key-Value
Fast lookups. Use for caches and simple mappings.
Document
Flexible schema. Use for user profiles and semi-structured records.
Column-Family
High write throughput and horizontal scale for time-series data.
Graph
Efficient relationship traversal for social or recommendation graphs.
Practical note

screens.title: Caches and CDNs: Reduce Latency and Load
screens.subtitle: When cached data reduces persistent store pressure

narration.text: Caches store frequently accessed data in faster storage, typically in-memory, to reduce latency and database load. There are multiple cache locations: client-side caches, CDNs for static assets and geographically distributed content, and server-side caches like Redis for application-level lookups. Apply cache selectively: cache results that are read-heavy and safe to serve for a short time, and avoid caching rapidly changing transactional data unless strong invalidation is in place. For a URL shortener, caching short_code to long_url mappings is a natural fit because redirections are read-heavy and the mapping changes rarely. A common misconception is that caching will always improve performance; poor cache eviction or stale data can cause correctness issues. Also avoid over-caching write-intensive endpoints. When you design caches, include a fallback path to the database and a clear invalidation policy so correctness is maintained. Consider how a CDN reduces geographic latency for static assets, but not for dynamic redirect logic unless edge caching is acceptable. Caches and CDNs: Reduce Latency and Load means use caches for read-heavy, low-volatility data; define invalidation and fallback strategies to preserve correctness.. In practical terms, when cached data reduces persistent store pressure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cache with intent
keyIdea.text: Use caches for read-heavy, low-volatility data; define invalidation and fallback strategies to preserve correctness.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Caches & CDNs
Cache types
  • Client-side: browser or app caches for quick retrieval.
  • CDN: geographic distribution for static assets and edge caching.
  • Server-side: Redis/Memcached for application lookups and sessions.
Example
Caching redirects in Redis reduces database reads for a URL shortener under high load.
Key Takeaway

Design a clear invalidation and fallback path to prevent stale reads when using caches.

Common pitfalls
Pitfall
Caching write-heavy or highly volatile data without careful invalidation causes stale or incorrect behavior.
Design note
Prefer caches for read-mostly flows and ensure a database fallback when cache misses occur.

screens.title: Message Queues and Asynchronous Processing
screens.subtitle: Decouple heavy work to keep user-facing flows responsive

narration.text: Message queues enable asynchronous communication between services and are essential when you need to decouple user-facing requests from heavy processing. The pattern is simple: the web/A P I service enqueues a task and returns quickly to the user, while a worker service consumes tasks and does the heavy lifting. This improves responsiveness and provides resilience: if workers are down, the queue buffers work until they catch up. Use queues for tasks like video encoding, analytics aggregation, or sending notifications. In the URL shortener, analytics or click counting can be produced by publishing redirection events to a queue consumed by an analytics service. A common misconception is that queues replace monitoring; they help buffer work but you still need visibility into backlog size and processing lag. Design your system to monitor queue depth and retry semantics, and plan for idempotency in consumers so retries don't duplicate effects. Ask: which user flows should be synchronous and which should be queued to meet latency targets? Message Queues and Asynchronous Processing means use queues to offload long-running tasks, buffer bursts, and improve user-perceived latency; monitor backlog and ensure idempotent consumers.. In practical terms, decouple heavy work to keep user-facing flows responsive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decouple heavy work
keyIdea.text: Use queues to offload long-running tasks, buffer bursts, and improve user-perceived latency; monitor backlog and ensure idempotent consumers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Message Queues
Queue pattern
  1. Producer enqueues a task and responds quickly to the client.
  2. Queue buffers tasks during bursts or when workers lag.
  3. Consumer processes tasks asynchronously and stores results.
Concrete example
When a user uploads a file, place a message with metadata on the queue; a separate worker handles resizing and storage.
Key Takeaway

Queues improve responsiveness and resilience, but require monitoring and idempotent consumers to avoid duplication.

Operational notes
Monitor
Track queue depth and processing lag to detect bottlenecks early.
Design for retries
Make consumers idempotent and plan retry and dead-letter handling for failed tasks.

screens.title: URL Shortener Example: Components and Flow
screens.subtitle: A concrete blueprint tying components to API endpoints

narration.text: Let’s apply the building blocks to a URL shortener. Clients submit a long URL and expect a short code in return, and later use that code for redirection. A typical architecture starts with a load balancer sending requests to stateless A P I servers. For POST /shorten the A P I generates a unique code and writes the mapping to durable storage. For GET /{short_code} the A P I first checks a cache for the mapping and falls back to the database on miss, then issues a redirect. Optional components include an analytics pipeline: on each redirect the A P I can publish an event to a message queue consumed by an analytics service that tallies clicks. Storage choice depends on scale and access: a relational DB is fine initially, and you can shard or move to a distributed store like Cassandra for very high write/read volumes. When describing this system, always tie each component to the concrete request path it serves and explain how it helps meet latency and availability goals. URL Shortener Example: Components and Flow means link each api endpoint to the components it uses so you can explain scaling and latency decisions for real request flows.. In practical terms, a concrete blueprint tying components to api endpoints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Map components to requests
keyIdea.text: Link each API endpoint to the components it uses so you can explain scaling and latency decisions for real request flows.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › URL Shortener Architecture
Block view
Client
Browser or app issues POST and GET requests.
Load Balancer → API Servers
Stateless servers generate codes and serve redirects.
Cache + Database
Redis serves hot lookups; DB stores durable mappings and can be sharded.
Optional Analytics
Publish redirect events to a queue consumed by analytics workers to count clicks without blocking redirects.
Example endpoints
POST /api/v1/urls
Accepts JSON {"longUrl": "https://..."}, returns shortUrl and 201 Created.
GET /{short_code}
Returns 302 Found with Location header pointing to the original URL, usually served after cache lookup.
Key Takeaway

Map each endpoint to the components it touches so you can argue scalability and latency trade-offs in interviews.

screens.title: Defining RESTful API Endpoints
screens.subtitle: Simple endpoints and expected responses for clarity

narration.text: When defining A P I endpoints, favor clear, resource-oriented paths and predictable responses. For the URL shortener, a POST to create a shortened URL and a GET to perform redirects are natural and simple. Being explicit about HTTP status codes and response bodies helps clients: POST returns 201 Created with the new short URL in JSON, while GET returns a 302 redirect with the location header. Keep payloads minimal and document required fields; for example, POST /api/v1/urls might accept a JSON payload containing a single longUrl field. In interviews, explain how these choices map to responsibilities: the A P I service validates input, writes the mapping, optionally populates a cache, and responds. Also discuss protocol choices: REST over HTTP is simple and widely understood; for internal services you might use RPC or gRPC when low-latency binary protocols are needed, but only if justified. A common misconception is that REST is always the best fit; choose the communication protocol that aligns with performance and interoperability requirements. Defining RESTful API Endpoints means design resource-focused endpoints with clear status semantics and minimal payloads so clients and services can interact predictably.. In practical terms, simple endpoints and expected responses for clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Simple, explicit APIs
keyIdea.text: Design resource-focused endpoints with clear status semantics and minimal payloads so clients and services can interact predictably.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › API Endpoints
Code-like examples
POST /api/v1/urls
Request body: {"longUrl": "https://verylongurl.com/..."}
Response: 201 Created
{
  "shortUrl": "http://short.ly/abcde"
}

GET /abcde
Response: 302 Found
Location: https://verylongurl.com/...
Design notes
  • Keep endpoints focused on a single responsibility and return explicit HTTP status codes.
  • Document required fields and error responses so clients can handle failures predictably.
Protocol choice
REST over HTTP is simple and widely adopted for public APIs. For low-latency, internal RPC you might consider other protocols, but only when justified by measurable needs.
Key Takeaway

Make endpoints explicit and justify protocol choices by performance and interoperability requirements.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls in High-Level Design
screens.subtitle: Avoid premature microservices and single-database assumptions

narration.text: Two frequent mistakes appear in early high-level designs. First, adding many microservices without justification increases operational complexity and cross-service communication. Microservices are valuable when teams, scaling, or independent failure domains require them; otherwise prefer a simpler monolith that can be split later. Second, assuming one relational database will suffice at scale is dangerous — a single DB can become a performance bottleneck and a single point of failure. Instead, plan for partitioning, replication, or polyglot persistence where different data types use different stores optimized for their patterns. Another mistake is neglecting caching or queues when read-heavy or bursty patterns exist; missing these can cause unacceptable latency or outages. When defending a design, state what you would add if load doubles, and why. That demonstrates that you think in terms of trade-offs and incremental complexity rather than over-engineering from day one. Common Mistakes and Pitfalls in High-Level Design means prefer simplicity until requirements justify complexity; always show how an added component maps to a measurable need.. In practical terms, avoid premature microservices and single-database assumptions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs over ornaments
keyIdea.text: Prefer simplicity until requirements justify complexity; always show how an added component maps to a measurable need.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Common Mistakes
Pitfall: Premature microservices

Splitting into many services before you understand load and ownership increases coordination costs and makes reliability harder to achieve.

Countermeasure
Start coarse, measure coupling and load, and split when performance or team ownership requires it.
Pitfall: Single database assumption

A single relational database can become a bottleneck. Plan for replication, sharding, or using specialized stores for different needs.

Countermeasure
Document how you'd partition data or introduce a second store and why that addresses the bottleneck.
Interview advice
When asked, present a simple system first, then explain one or two targeted changes you'd make for higher load, and the trade-offs each change introduces.

screens.title: Design Exercise: Notification Service
screens.subtitle: Apply high-level design to a system that sends email, SMS, and push notifications

narration.text: This activity asks you to translate requirements into a block diagram for a notification service that must send email, SMS, and push notifications at scale. Start by listing the main components: clients, a load balancer, a Notification A P I, a message queue, and separate sender services for each channel. The Notification A P I validates requests and enqueues tasks rather than sending synchronously. Worker services consume the queue and call provider APIs for email, SMS, or push. Store templates and user preferences in a database so senders can personalize messages. The queue buffers bursts and lets you scale senders independently. When writing an example A P I, define POST /send_notification with fields for recipient, channel, templateId, and payload. Justify the queue: it keeps the A P I responsive and isolates retry and failure logic in workers. Finally, when you draw the diagram, label each component’s role and note one operational metric you would monitor, such as queue depth or success rate. That practice makes your design defendable and measurable. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, high-level design is a blueprint that maps requirements and scale to major components and interactions; your diagrams should be justifiable and measurable. Second, the load balancer and stateless web tier form the backbone of a horizontally scalable service; state belongs in external stores. Third, choose storage based on access patterns — S Q L for transactions and NoSQL families for lookup, flexible schemas, scale, or graph needs. Fourth, caches and CDNs reduce latency for read-heavy workloads, while message queues decouple long-running work and improve responsiveness. Finally, define clear A P I endpoints and communication protocols so services interact predictably. Keep designs simple until complexity is warranted and always tie every component to a concrete requirement or performance goal. Which one of these concepts will you focus on practicing this week?

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Blueprint, storage fit, and decoupling are the pillars of strong high-level system design.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Key Concepts
High-Level Design (HLD)
An initial blueprint showing major components and interactions guided by requirements.
Core Components
Load balancers, web/API servers, databases, caches, and message queues form the core blocks you will use.
APIs and Protocols
Define clear endpoints and response semantics; match protocol choices to performance and interoperability needs.
Bottom Line
Design simply, justify each component by a measurable requirement, and be ready to explain trade-offs in an interview setting.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to carry into interviews

narration.text: Keep these three short mental anchors. First, tie every architectural decision to a requirement or a measured estimate — that is how you justify complexity. Second, prefer stateless services behind load balancers and externalize durable state to appropriate stores; this keeps scaling straightforward. Third, use caches and queues where they directly address latency or burst handling. When you rehearse designs, always name the metric you would monitor to validate the design, such as request latency, queue depth, or cache hit rate. These anchors help you explain your design succinctly and show practical reasoning during interviews. Which metric will you use to validate your next design? What to Remember means justify components with metrics, prefer statelessness, and use caches/queues to meet latency and burst requirements.. In practical terms, three compact cards to carry into interviews. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interview anchors
keyIdea.text: Justify components with metrics, prefer statelessness, and use caches/queues to meet latency and burst requirements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › What to Remember
Justify with metrics
Always tie components to measurable requirements like latency or RPS.
Stateless servers
Keep application servers stateless and place state in services that scale independently.
Use caches & queues
Employ caches for read-heavy paths and queues to decouple heavy processing from user flows.
Final thought
When you present a high-level design, walk through one user request and state how each component helps meet a measurable target.
